title: Epochal Backstop Credit Allocator — PRD (idea)
content:
Purpose:
This doc outlines a concept for a tenant credit allocator that operates in fixed epochs to manage Dedicated pool burst capacity and soft isolation. The goal is to let tenants borrow headroom predictably, enforce fairness across noisy neighbors, and provide an operational backstop lane for emergency bursts with minimal manual intervention.

Problem statement:
- Tenants on Dedicated pools experience unpredictable microbursts that either: (a) cause latency SLO violations for other tenants, or (b) force heavy-handed global throttles that reduce utilization and customer satisfaction.
- Existing approaches (strict reservations, static overprovisioning, or purely reactive preemption) are either too expensive or too disruptive.
- We need a middle ground that enables temporary overcommit with controlled cost, clear billing semantics, and automatic recovery.

High-level proposal:
- Introduce an "Epochal Backstop" credit model: time is divided into short epochs (e.g., 5m). Each tenant has a primary reserved capacity and an epoch-scoped credit bucket that can be consumed for bursts.
- Credits refill slowly (longer half-life) to avoid repeated long-duration debt cycles; a small portion of reserved capacity can be converted into burst credits for short-term elasticity.
- A global backstop lane provides emergency capacity (paid or free depending on plan) that can be consumed when epoch buckets are exhausted; backstop use triggers stricter QoS controls and additional telemetry/alerts.

Goals (measurable):
- Reduce cross-tenant latency SLO breaches during bursts by 50% in simulated mixed workloads.
- Allow average Dedicated cluster utilization to increase by 8–12% without increasing customer-observed tail latency.
- Provide billing clarity: burst credit consumption is visible per-epoch and appears as a distinct line item.

Non-goals:
- Not intended to replace long-term reserved capacity contracts or enterprise SLAs with guaranteed headroom.
- Not a substitute for per-model/route request shaping; application-level throttles still recommended.

User stories:
- As an SRE for a mid-market customer, I want predictable, short bursts for traffic spikes so my application retains latency SLAs without constant over-reserving.
- As an account owner, I want to see per-epoch credit usage and be billed clearly for backstop consumption.
- As Redwood operator, I want automatic reclaim policies and diagnostics to troubleshoot noisy tenants.

Key concepts and primitives:
- Epoch: contiguous time window (configurable, default 5m) during which credits are consumed/reported.
- Reserved Capacity: committed pool for tenant baseline throughput.
- Epoch Credits: per-tenant token bucket (credits) that deplete as tenant uses burst capacity; refill rate is slow (e.g., 1 credit per N epochs) to limit abuse.
- Soft Commit: temporary admission into additional capacity based on available credits and local per-worker admission rules. Softly committed requests can be preempted if absolute SLO thresholds for other tenants approach.
- Backstop Lane: shared emergency capacity with stricter isolation and auditing; usage may be metered at premium rates or gated by support plan.

Admission and isolation policy (sketch):
1) Normal path: requests served from reserved capacity.
2) If reserved capacity exhausted, consult epoch credits. If credits available and local worker has spare GPU cycles, accept as soft commit and decrement credits. 3) If no credits, consult backstop lane. If backstop allowed for tenant and pool has capacity, admit with strict QoS: lower concurrency, higher risk of preemption, and extra tracing enabled. 4) If backstop exhausted, apply shed/throttle policy (short tail-drop or 429 with retry-after).

Fairness and arbitration rules:
- Weighted fairness across tenants by reserved units; epoch credit caps prevent sustained overuse.
- A small probabilistic preemption policy enables gentle reclaim: soft-committed requests flagged with an eviction-score; workers periodically evict lowest-score tasks under pressure instead of abrupt global cutoffs.
- A short random jitter on refill timings reduces synchronized bursts across tenants.

Billing and economics:
- Display per-epoch credit consumption and backstop MB-minutes/tokens in Console.
- Pricing model options to explore: free small credit pool per billing period + pay-as-you-go backstop; tiered burst allowances for enterprise contracts; discounted backstop for long-term reserved customers.

Telemetry and observability:
- New metrics: epoch_credit_balance, epoch_credit_consumed, soft_commits_per_epoch, backstop_consumption, preemption_evictions, per-tenant tail-latency-during-burst.
- Console dashboards: per-pool heatmap, top burst consumers, anomalies by epoch.
- Alerts: when a tenant's epoch credit drops below a threshold and when backstop usage exceeds projected capacity for 3 consecutive epochs.

Simulation plan:
- Build a discrete-event simulator that models tenants with: baseline qps, burst frequency, burst amplitude, and refill profile.
- Run mixed tenant mixes (SaaS multi-tenant, single large tenant, many small tenants) and measure: tail latency impact, credit exhaustion events, and utilization uplift.
- Compare against baseline strategies: strict reservation, opportunistic first-come, and global preempt-on-overload.

Rollout strategy:
- Phase 0: Simulation + bench experiments in dev clusters.
- Phase 1: Opt-in alpha for a small set of customers (non-critical workloads) with fine-grained telemetry and manual rollback.
- Phase 2: Wider beta with billing preview and user-configurable epoch length/credit strategy.
- Phase 3: GA with default conservative parameters and enterprise-configurable policies.

Operational runbook (high-level):
- If backstop consumption spikes: alert ops and run automated mitigation: temporarily increase epoch throttles, lower refill rate, or enable additional preemption aggressiveness.
- If a tenant repeatedly exhausts credits: suggest tenant upgrade path or recommend dedicated extra reservation.
- Failure modes: credit accounting drift — run reconciliation daily and pause backstop until corrected.

Risks and open questions:
- Complexity: adds cognitive overhead for customers and ops; must surface defaults that "just work".
- Gaming the system: tenants could spread load across multiple accounts to multiply bursts — need enterprise guardrails.
- Billing disputes: accurate per-epoch metering is critical.
- Interaction with cache/KV warm pools: bursts that benefit from warm caches may have different cost/latency profiles and need adjusted credit weighting.

Next steps (immediate):
- Align with infra (serving-runtime) on necessary worker-level admission hooks and eviction scoring.
- Product + Finance to propose 2 pricing variants for backstop.
- Start small-scale simulator and a baking plan for alpha customers.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally a sketch to capture an intermediate design space between hard reservations and unconditional over-commit. Focus review on: fairness constraints, clear observable signals, and billing clarity.

Unresolved design decisions (short list):
- Default epoch length (5m vs 1m vs 10m).
- Exact refill curve (linear vs exponential decay/half-life).
- Whether backstop should be gated behind support tiers or available to all with billing.
